flawed_step: Step 5: the bound |N(S)| ≥ |S|/2 is incorrectly strengthened to Hall’s required bound |N(S)| ≥ |S|.
counterexample: Let A={a1,a2}, B={b}, and E={{a1,b},{a2,b}}. Both vertices of A have degree 1, and b has degree 2, but a matching contains at most one edge and therefore cannot saturate A.
assessment_summary:
1. Let S⊆A and let N(S) be its neighborhood in B. — JUSTIFIED: this is standard notation for an arbitrary subset of A.
2. Because every vertex in S has degree at least 1, at least |S| edges join S to N(S). — JUSTIFIED: summing the degrees of vertices in S counts precisely those incident edges and gives at least |S|.
3. Because every vertex of B has degree at most 2, at most 2|N(S)| edges join S to N(S). — JUSTIFIED: each vertex of N(S) is incident with at most two such edges.
4. Consequently, |S|≤2|N(S)|, so |N(S)|≥|S|/2. — JUSTIFIED: this follows directly from Steps 2 and 3.
5. Attempt to infer |N(S)|≥|S| for every S⊆A, as required by Hall’s condition. — NOT JUSTIFIED: Step 4 supplies only the weaker lower bound |S|/2; the degree hypotheses do not imply Hall’s condition.
6. Attempt to apply Hall’s marriage theorem to obtain a matching saturating A. — NOT JUSTIFIED: Hall’s neighborhood condition was not established in Step 5.
7. Take A={a1,a2}, B={b}, with edges a1b and a2b. — JUSTIFIED: every A-vertex has degree 1 and the sole B-vertex has degree 2, so all stated hypotheses hold.
8. No matching in this graph saturates A. — JUSTIFIED: its two edges share b, so a matching can contain at most one of them and can cover at most one A-vertex.
9. Therefore the proposed statement is false. — JUSTIFIED: Steps 7–8 give a counterexample satisfying every hypothesis while violating the conclusion.
